scenes.heading: Covalent bonding and molecular shape
scenes.sub: How sharing electrons decides a molecule's shape
scenes.say: Water, carbon dioxide, plastics and medicines are all held together by covalent bonds. The way atoms share electrons decides a molecule's shape, and that shape decides how it behaves.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Two players both gripping the same footy
scenes.science: Two nuclei both attracted to a shared pair of electrons
scenes.breaks: electrons aren't a solid ball in one spot; they're spread out as a cloud of negative charge.
scenes.say: Picture two players both gripping the same footy, and neither will let go. The footy is the shared pair of electrons, and the players are the two nuclei. Both are pulled towards the same ball, and that holds them together. That's a covalent bond.

scenes.heading: Covalent bonds
points: Non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons
Most atoms reach an octet (H needs 2)
HONC 1234: H 1, O 2, N 3, C 4 bonds
scenes.say: When two non-metals bond, they share pairs of electrons: one pair for a single bond, two for a double, three for a triple. Remember HONC one two three four: hydrogen makes one bond, oxygen two, nitrogen three, carbon four.

scenes.heading: VSEPR: predicting the shape
steps: Count electron groups on central atom
Groups push as far apart as possible
Lone pairs push harder, squeeze angles
Name the shape from the atoms only
scenes.say: VSEPR theory says electron pairs around the central atom push as far apart as they can. Lone pairs push a bit harder and squeeze the angles. But you name the shape from the atoms only.

scenes.heading: Four electron groups
scenes.say: With four electron groups and no lone pairs, like methane, you get tetrahedral, one hundred and nine point five degrees. One lone pair, like ammonia, gives pyramidal. Two lone pairs, like water, give bent.
scenes.caption: With four electron groups and no lone pairs, like CH₄, you get tetrahedral, 109.5°. One lone pair, like NH₃, gives pyramidal. Two lone pairs, like H₂O, give bent.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: What is the shape of PCl₃, and is it polar?
lines: 3 P–Cl bonding pairs + 1 lone pair on P
P–Cl bonds are polar; shape is asymmetric
scenes.say: What shape is P C l three? There are twenty-six valence electrons, so thirteen pairs. Phosphorus gets three bonding pairs and one lone pair. Four groups with one lone pair means pyramidal. The bonds are polar and the shape isn't symmetrical, so it's polar.
scenes.caption: What shape is PCl₃? There are 26 valence electrons, so 13 pairs. P gets 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair. Four groups with one lone pair means pyramidal. The bonds are polar and the shape isn't symmetrical, so it's polar.

scenes.heading: Is the molecule polar?
points: Polar bond: atoms differ in electronegativity
CO₂ is linear, so it's non-polar
Bent H₂O doesn't cancel, so it's polar
scenes.say: Polarity is a tug-of-war. A bond is polar when the atoms differ in electronegativity, but the molecule is only polar if the pulls don't cancel. Linear carbon dioxide cancels, so it's non-polar. Bent water doesn't, so it's polar.

points: Covalent bond = shared pair of electrons
Electron groups spread as far apart as possible
Name shapes from atoms, not lone pairs
scenes.say: Quick recap. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. Electron groups spread as far apart as they can, which sets the shape. Name the shape from the atoms, not the lone pairs. Polar bonds plus an uneven shape make a polar molecule. Now try the practice questions!
